articles.title: Sydney Sweeney bought a $6.2 million 1930s Bel-Air estate on 1.25 acres; she wanted to restore its overgrown garden without erasing its old Hollywood character
articles.summary: A vine-covered mansion in Bel-Air might seem like an obvious candidate for a complete renovation, particularly when its new owner is a Hollywood actor
articles.body: A vine-covered mansion in Bel-Air might seem like an obvious candidate for a complete renovation, particularly when its new owner is a Hollywood actor with the means to start afresh. Sydney Sweeney had a different approach when she bought a property dating back to the 1930s in 2023. Rather than stripping away its aged features to create a freshly remodelled luxury home, she wanted to retain the qualities that gave it a connection to an earlier period of Hollywood. According to Architectural Digest, the estate, set on 1.25 acres, came with an overgrown garden, persistent vines and a house in poor condition. Sweeney saw the work ahead as a chance to restore the property without making its history disappear.Sydney Sweeney paid $6.2 million for a historic Bel-Air estateSweeney paid $6.2 million for the Bel-Air estate in 2023, adding a substantial renovation project to a property portfolio that already included her first home in Los Angeles. The mansion was built in the 1930s and had a connection to Hollywood's Golden Age through its former association with the family of screenwriter and director Delmer Daves, known for films including 3:10 to Yuma.The two-storey residence covers approximately 4,477 square feet and has five bedrooms and four bathrooms. The grounds extend across 1.25 acres, giving the house considerably more outdoor space than a typical city property. A separate guesthouse and swimming pool are also part of the estate.As reported by Architectural Digest, the property had last changed hands in 1984 before Sweeney's purchase. She reportedly secured it after competing with other interested buyers. Its condition, however, meant that moving straight in was not an option.An overgrown garden and a plan to preserve Hollywood historyWhen Sweeney showed Glamour around the house in October 2024, the grounds looked far removed from the carefully maintained gardens commonly associated with expensive Los Angeles estates. Vines covered parts of the building, while the garden had become overgrown. The house itself was in such poor condition that it could not be occupied during the renovation.For Sweeney, the answer was not to remove every trace of age and replace it with contemporary finishes. She explained that she wanted the work to respect what was already there, rather than leave visitors wondering when the original house had been remodelled. She said,"We'll fix it up as much as we can without hurting any of it.”She also made clear that the finished property should retain a sense of continuity with its past. "I want it to feel timeless, like it is."Her comments set out the distinction between restoring an older building and remaking it entirely. The estate needed substantial attention, but its aged appearance and historic details were not simply problems to be eliminated. The garden's untamed state was part of the wider picture of a house that had spent decades accumulating its own character.Sydney Sweeney wanted the estate’s Hollywood history to stay intactSweeney's interest in the property's history extended beyond its exterior. Before she completed the purchase, she was filming ‘Anyone But You’ in Australia, so her mother went to the estate sale on her behalf. Sweeney asked her to buy the contents of the former owner's office, hoping the material could remain associated with the house.The collection included Hollywood memorabilia and signed items connected to celebrated figures from the film industry. During the Glamour visit, Sweeney discussed discovering pieces associated with actors such as Cary Grant and Clark Gable. These objects offered a tangible link to an earlier generation of Hollywood, complementing the property's own history.That approach also helps explain why she did not want a renovation that made the building feel entirely new. The aim was to improve the house while retaining the details and associations that made it different from a recently constructed luxury residence.The condition of the property meant that preservation would not be a matter of leaving everything untouched. Repairs were necessary, and the estate would have to be made suitable for modern use. Sweeney's stated preference was to carry out that work without losing the qualities that had attracted her to the house in the first place.Inside Sydney Sweeney’s first Los Angeles home in WestwoodWhile the Bel-Air mansion remained uninhabitable, Sweeney continued to stay at the Tudor-style house she bought in 2021 for approximately $3 million. Located in Westwood, the property was built in 1933 and measures around 3,200 square feet, as reported. It has five bedrooms, four bathrooms, vaulted wooden-beam ceilings and original brick fireplaces.Sweeney has given the house the affectionate nickname "Snow White's château". Its character differs from that of the Bel-Air estate, but both properties have older architectural features that distinguish them from more contemporary homes.The Westwood purchase also marked a personal milestone for the actor. In an interview with The Associated Press in 2021, she spoke about the significance of finally owning a home after her family's financial difficulties during her early years in Los Angeles.By the time she bought the Bel-Air property, Sweeney had established herself through roles in Euphoria, The White Lotus and The Handmaid's Tale, alongside her work in films. Her growing career had given her the means to purchase a more expensive estate, but the way she discussed its renovation suggested that the decision was not based on size or price alone.Why preserving the old Hollywood feel mattersSweeney's Bel-Air project sits at the intersection of property investment and historic preservation. Older homes in Los Angeles can be renovated in ways that retain their original architectural features, or altered so extensively that much of their previous identity disappears. Her public comments indicated a preference for the former, even though the house required significant work.The overgrown garden, vines and deteriorated interiors presented practical challenges, but they also formed part of the estate's appearance when she bought it. The task was to decide what needed repairing and what deserved to remain. Sweeney did not describe a plan to preserve every feature exactly as it was; instead, she spoke about improving the house without damaging its existing character.As of her October 2024 Glamour profile, the mansion was still undergoing the process of being made liveable. The finished result had yet to be revealed in that account, so the full extent of the restoration and any changes to the grounds remained unclear.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: In 2004, Shannen Doherty paid $2.56 million for a Malibu home she called her sanctuary; 22 years later, after a $9.5 million posthumous listing and price cut, the property sold for $7.65 million
articles.summary: Shannen Doherty’s longtime Malibu home has sold for $7.65 million, nearly two years after the actress died following a lengthy battle with cancer.
articles.body: Shannen Doherty’s longtime Malibu home has sold for $7.65 million, nearly two years after the actress died following a lengthy battle with cancer. Doherty bought the five-bedroom property for $2.56 million in 2004 and later described it as a private sanctuary where she could escape the demands of Hollywood. The home was listed for $9.5 million in August 2025, more than a year after her death, but attracted a buyer only after several price reductions. Realtor.com reported that the property eventually went under contract after its asking price was reduced to $8.25 million. The final sale closed for $600,000 below that figure, ending the Malibu chapter of a home closely associated with Doherty’s personal life.A private refuge in MalibuDoherty purchased the property after establishing herself through major television roles in Beverly Hills, 90210 and Charmed. At the time, she was already familiar with the pressures of public attention, making privacy an important part of the home’s appeal. The actress found that privacy behind mature hedging on one of Malibu’s desirable streets. The estate covers approximately one acre and includes 5,400 square feet of living space. Its location offered a sense of seclusion while still providing the natural beauty and ocean views associated with Malibu.Doherty’s longtime friend Chris Cortazzo, who listed the property and served as executor of her estate, explained to the Wall Street Journal why the home mattered to her. As reported by Realtor.com, Cortazzo said that when someone is a notable figure, a home can become a sanctuary.The property was also a place where Doherty welcomed a small circle of friends. Cortazzo recalled that she hosted regular Italian Nights and Dancing Nights, creating traditions that made the house feel less like a celebrity residence and more like a comfortable gathering place.Renovated after the Woolsey FireThe property was damaged during the Woolsey Fire in 2018, which affected parts of Malibu and surrounding areas. Doherty later carried out an extensive renovation, rebuilding the home while retaining many of the features that gave it its character, as per the report.It further shared that the exterior combines stucco walls with large sections of glass. Those glass walls open the rear of the residence towards the surrounding landscape and provide expansive views from the main living areas. The primary suite includes a retractable glass wall that strengthens the connection between the bedroom and the outdoors.Inside, the design balances a neutral colour palette with warmer and more personal elements. Beamed ceilings add texture to the living areas, while the kitchen features custom cabinetry and a spacious layout. Sliding barn doors separate the dining room from the den, giving the interiors a rustic detail that contrasts with the home’s modern architecture.Cortazzo also said that the property contained treasures Doherty had collected while travelling. These objects helped make the renovated house feel personal rather than overly staged for the luxury market.Resort-style outdoor spaceThe grounds were one of the most important features of the estate. A lap pool with an integrated spa overlooks the ocean and provides a natural centre for the outdoor areas. Privacy hedges surround the property, protecting the gardens and entertaining spaces from public view.The landscaping includes tiered gardens, mature trees and a dining terrace designed for meals outdoors. An edible garden with raised beds and fruit trees adds a practical element to the grounds, giving the property a connection to nature beyond its decorative landscaping.A detached guesthouse sits separately from the main residence. It could be used as a private guest suite, a studio, an extra bedroom or a fitness space. That flexibility increased the property’s appeal for buyers looking for a home that could support both private living and entertaining.The listing described the estate as a combination of California modernism and rustic refinement. It presented the home as a place designed around natural light, indoor-outdoor movement and a calm atmosphere.A difficult saleDoherty’s estate first placed the property on the market for $9.5 million in August 2025. That price was almost four times what she had paid in 2004, although it also reflected the renovation, the land, the views and the size of the residence.The home did not sell immediately. The asking price was reduced several times, eventually reaching $8.25 million in February. Realtor.com later reported that the property had gone pending, although the terms of the offer were not initially disclosed.The final sale price was $7.65 million, which was $600,000 below the last asking price. Compared with Doherty’s original purchase price, the property sold for approximately $5.09 million more, reported Relator.com. The difference does not represent pure profit because it does not account for renovation costs, taxes, maintenance, commissions or other expenses connected with owning and selling the home.Wildfire concerns may also have influenced the pace of the sale. Although the estate was outside the Malibu area affected by the January 2025 California wildfires, buyers had reportedly become more cautious about fire risk. Cortazzo said prospective owners were paying close attention to brush clearance, roofing materials and other safety factors before committing to properties in the region.Proceeds to go to her motherBecause Doherty had no children, proceeds from the sale are expected to go to her mother, Rosa, according to Cortazzo. Doherty was still legally married to photographer Kurt Iswarienko when she died, although the couple had separated in 2023. Their divorce was finalised two days after her death.The sale therefore carried an emotional and practical significance beyond its financial value. It involved the handling of an estate after the death of an actress who had spoken openly about her health, relationships and plans for the future.Doherty was diagnosed with Stage 3 breast cancer in 2015. She later revealed that the cancer had returned and progressed to Stage 4. Through interviews and her Let’s Be Clear podcast, she discussed treatment, fear, hope and her determination to continue living fully.The Malibu home became especially important during those years. It offered a protected space where Doherty could spend time with people close to her and step away from the attention surrounding her illness and career.The end of a meaningful chapterThe sale of Doherty’s Malibu residence closes the story of a house that served as much more than a luxury asset. It was where she created private traditions, rebuilt after a devastating fire and found a measure of calm during an intensely difficult period of her life.For the buyer, the estate offers ocean views, mature landscaping, a lap pool, a guesthouse and a carefully renovated interior. For those who followed Doherty’s career, however, it will remain associated with the actress’s idea of home as a place of protection and connection.Purchased for $2.56 million in 2004, listed for $9.5 million after her death and ultimately sold for $7.65 million, the property has now entered a new chapter. Its next owner will inherit a secluded Malibu estate, while Doherty’s family receives the proceeds from the home she once considered her sanctuary.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Makeup, colourful scarves, speaking in public: Bizarre reasons women get detained in Afghanistan
articles.summary: Afghanistan’s Taliban authorities detained 52 women and one girl between July and September for alleged dress code violations and appearing in public
articles.body: Afghanistan’s Taliban authorities detained 52 women and one girl between July and September for alleged dress code violations and appearing in public without a male guardian, including for wearing makeup, colourful scarves or leaving their hair visible, the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) said on Thursday.The arrests were reported in Kabul and the western city of Herat. UNAMA said it was “gravely concerned” about the detentions and threats of arrest, warning that safety concerns and stigma could mean many more cases had gone unreported. It also raised alarm over reports of verbal abuse, beatings and threats against women, including female shopkeepers. The Taliban government did not immediately respond to the statement.What can get women detained under Taliban rule?The reasons cited in the latest cases offer a glimpse of how closely the Taliban police women’s appearance and movement in public. Women were reportedly detained for not wearing a chador, leaving their hair visible, wearing colourful scarves or makeup, or going out without a mahram, a close male relative who acts as a guardian.These restrictions sit alongside the Taliban’s 2024 Law on the Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice, which lays out detailed requirements for women’s clothing and conduct. Article 13 says women must cover their entire bodies and states that they should cover their faces to prevent fitna. It also requires women to conceal their voices in certain public settings, including singing, reciting or chanting aloud in gatherings.The law further says women’s clothing must not be thin, short or tight, and that women must conceal their bodies and faces from men who are not close male relatives. It also says an adult woman leaving home for an urgent need must conceal her voice, face and body.The law applies across Afghanistan and provides for a sequence of enforcement measures, ranging from warnings and fines to detention. The translated text also allows enforcers to impose other punishments they consider appropriate, subject to the law’s stated conditions.A wider crackdown on womenSince returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have imposed sweeping restrictions on women and girls, including barring girls from education beyond primary school and curbing women’s movement and participation in public life.The latest detentions come months after Taliban authorities opened fire on a rare protest in Herat in June over the arrest of women for alleged dress code violations. At least one person was killed and several others were wounded, according to witnesses and UNAMA.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: China opens military base at former CIA airfield in Laos
articles.summary: China has opened a new military outpost at a former CIA-operated airfield in northwestern Laos, adding to Beijing’s defence cooperation with the Southeast
articles.body: China has opened a new military outpost at a former CIA-operated airfield in northwestern Laos, adding to Beijing’s defence cooperation with the Southeast Asian nation. The facility, which began operations on September 29, is located around 40 miles north of the capital Vientiane and 25 miles from the nearest border with Thailand, CNN reported.The outpost comprises the China-Laos Joint Support and Training Center at Ban Keun Airport and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy. China’s defence ministry said the facilities would help Laos train and develop its air force pilots and would be jointly maintained by the two countries.Satellite imagery obtained by CNN from intelligence platform Vantor shows that a 6,500-foot runway, taxiway and parking apron capable of accommodating 22 aircraft have been completed since December. Eight aircraft, possibly Hongdu JL-8 jets used for training and light-attack missions, are visible in the images.China’s defence ministry said the facilities were “not directed against any third party and are conducive to further strengthening practical cooperation between the two militaries and maintaining regional peace and stability.”The site previously served as a logistics and support hub for Air America, the CIA-operated airline used during the Vietnam War for covert operations in the region. Its transformation into a Chinese military facility carries historical significance, although analysts cited in the report said it does not indicate a major shift in the US-China military balance.Drew Thompson, a senior fellow at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said it was difficult to see how the base could threaten US forces in the region. “This runway is not a dagger pointed at the heart of anything,” Thompson said. He also questioned the operational value of launching aircraft from the site, given its proximity to Thailand, a major non-NATO ally of the US.Rachel Vandenbrink, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, told Reuters that China’s selection of Ban Keun “is likely more about a target of opportunity than filling an obvious operational need.” She said Laos could offer Beijing a strategic foothold in mainland Southeast Asia because of its shared border with China and infrastructure links, including a railway.China currently has one officially acknowledged overseas military base, in Djibouti, which opened in 2017. Beijing has also funded a major expansion of Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base on the Gulf of Thailand, which it operates jointly with the Cambodian military. A new pier capable of accommodating Chinese aircraft carriers has raised concerns about Beijing’s intentions, although Cambodia says the facility remains open to other countries, including the US.You use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Delhi Police has denied permission for the Cockroach Janata Party’s (CJP) proposed protest at Jantar Mantar on October 10, citing the late submission of its application, non-compliance with rules during a previous demonstration and concerns over public safety, law and order, and traffic management.Addressing a press conference, Joint Commissioner of Police Nupur Prasad said the New Delhi district police received an application from CJP co-convenor Saurabh Das on October 7, seeking permission to hold a protest demanding accountability from Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.“On October 7, 2026, an application from Saurabh Das, Co-Convenor of the Cockroach Janata Party, was received in the New Delhi District. As per the application, an intimation was given regarding a protest to be held at Jantar Mantar on October 10 concerning the accountability of the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC). Under current guidelines, an application to organise an event at Jantar Mantar must be submitted at least 10 days prior to the scheduled date. It is also important to note that, based on the past conduct of the CJP on a separate occasion, undertakings and lawful directions given previously were not followed," Prasad said."In light of the non-compliance with prescribed procedures, the failure to adhere to past legal directions, and the current state of public safety, law and order, and traffic regulation, permission for the proposed protest at Jantar Mantar is hereby denied,” she added.Meanwhile, the Supreme Court has rejected a plea seeking directions to give Delhi Police a free hand to deal with protesters, observing that the future of young students and their families must be considered in such matters.A bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said many protesters were young and should not be unnecessarily drawn into prolonged court proceedings.“These are young students and protesters before us. articles.title: ‘About 100 H-1B visa holders were on Amazon’s initial team that built AWS’: Ex-employee criticises US green-card suspension for tech firms
articles.summary: Shobhit Mathur, co-founder and vice-chancellor of Rishihood University, has defended the contribution of skilled foreign workers to the US technology
articles.body: Shobhit Mathur, co-founder and vice-chancellor of Rishihood University, has defended the contribution of skilled foreign workers to the US technology industry, recalling his experience of joining Amazon on an H-1B visa when the company was still making losses. In a post on X, Mathur said he was part of the initial team that built Amazon Web Services (AWS), adding that approximately 100 H-1B visa holders were involved in Amazon’s early team. His account comes amid renewed debate over skilled immigration after the US administration announced restrictions on green-card sponsorship processing for several technology companies.Ex-employee shares Amazon’s journey: From makeshift desks to a technology giantMathur recalled that Amazon was operating from a rented building when he joined, with employees working at makeshift desks made from doors inside small cabins. He said the company was making losses at the time and that around 100 H-1B visa holders were part of its initial team. According to Mathur, these professionals contributed their hard work and expertise to building the foundations of Amazon Web Services (AWS), which has since grown into one of the company’s most significant sources of profit.Mathur’s central argument is that foreign professionals can contribute to building businesses that eventually generate substantial economic value. He pointed to AWS as an example, saying that the cloud-computing business has become a major source of Amazon’s profits and helped transform the company’s financial position.AWS has become a major source of Amazon’s profitsAmazon’s published results show the scale of the business Mathur describes. In 2025, AWS generated $128.7 billion in net sales, up 20% from the previous year, and its operating income rose to $45.6 billion from $39.8 billion in 2024. Amazon’s total operating income for the year was $80.0 billion, making AWS responsible for about 57% of it, even though it accounted for roughly 18% of the company’s $716.9 billion in net sales.The share has since climbed past the level Mathur cites. In the second quarter of 2026, AWS sales rose 37% to $42.2 billion and its operating income reached $16.6 billion, or about 60.5% of Amazon’s total operating income.US suspends PERM labour certification for major technology firmsMathur’s comments come as the Trump administration has intensified scrutiny of employment-based immigration. On October 8, 2026, Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the suspension alongside Vice-President JD Vance. The Department of Labor suspended eight companies from the Permanent Labour Certification programme, known as PERM: Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe.PERM is a labour certification process generally required for employment-based green-card applications. Employers typically must demonstrate that there are not sufficient able, willing, qualified and available US workers for the position and that employing a foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed US workers.The department said it would not accept new PERM applications or process pending ones from the named companies. The reasons differed by company. Sonderling said the six outsourcing firms were suspended outright, while Microsoft and Adobe were suspended due to multiple active federal investigations. Vance singled out Microsoft, saying it laid off 6,000 American workers last year while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards. Reuters reported that Microsoft is the largest filer of PERM applications, based on Permtrack.app data. TCS said in an exchange filing that it would follow any directions issued by the Department of Labor.Why H-1B visas are at the centre of the debateThe H-1B programme allows US employers to hire foreign professionals for specialty occupations that generally require highly specialised knowledge and a relevant bachelor’s degree or equivalent qualifications. Technology companies use it to recruit software engineers, researchers and other skilled workers from international talent pools.Amazon has been a major participant. One summary of Pew Research Center’s analysis reports that Amazon came first with 11,000 H-1B approvals in 2023. More recently, Amazon’s approvals rose from 9,257 in 2024 to 10,044 in 2025, and a letter from US senators described the FY2025 figure as nearly double that of the next-highest employer. These counts include extensions and transfers, so they do not measure new foreign hires.The programme has also faced criticism over whether some employers use foreign workers to reduce labour costs or replace American employees. The US Department of Labor requires employers hiring H-1B workers to pay at least the higher of the actual wage paid to similarly qualified employees or the prevailing wage for the occupation and location. The department can investigate alleged violations of these requirements.The administration argues that restrictions are necessary to address cases of alleged wage undercutting and displacement. Technology companies and advocates of skilled immigration argue that access to international talent helps businesses recruit specialised workers and develop new products. articles.title: At 21, an Australian waitress quit with $100 and cooked meals for 10 gym friends from a Bondi apartment; the side hustle later reached $5 million in revenue and built a 100-acre farm
articles.summary: Bianca Monley was 21, had little more than $100, a tiny Bondi apartment and an instinct that healthy food could be more exciting than what was available
articles.body: Bianca Monley was 21, had little more than $100, a tiny Bondi apartment and an instinct that healthy food could be more exciting than what was available at the time. She quit her waitress job and started cooking meals for 10 friends from the gym in her area. There was no big business plan, no investors, just a kitchen, a handful of customers and the desire to see where the idea might lead. That little experiment was now a $5 million business and a 100-acre farm years later. Scroll down for details.Begin with clarityMonley’s first step was understanding what she wanted the business to achieve, she said on her website. The idea was simple. Help people eat better. As the company grew, that purpose developed into a larger mission to change the perception around healthy food. That clarity became a filter for decisions from what products to offer to how the business connected with customers. Any entrepreneur can use an understanding of why the business exists to decide what is important to pay attention to and what is not.Create a memorable thingA strong brand is much more than just a recognizable logo. It’s what customers think of when they think about a business. Monley’s company set itself apart by providing fresh meals delivered to homes and developing its own farm to create a direct link between food production and the customer. The farm-to-table concept gave the business a distinct identity and reinforced its commitment to freshness, quality and sustainability. Consistency from packaging to customer service helped convert first-time buyers into loyal customers.Hustle, then learn how to delegateMonley did practically everything in the beginning. From cooking, packing, deliveries, to making money. That hands-on approach was necessary when the business was small, but it could not be the model forever. As the company expanded to include Melbourne and Sydney and grow a 100 acre farm, it was necessary to bring in specialists. The founder could walk away from day-to-day chores and focus on growth, because of chefs, nutritionists, gardeners and other professionals. And the lesson was simple: hard work can build a business, but delegation is what scales it.View setbacks as lessonsThe path of entrepreneurship rarely moves straight up. Monley’s journey included financial pressure, long nights, and tough decisions. Instead of seeing these moments as failures, she used them as a way to figure out what needed to change.The company got a big break when actor Hugh Jackman became a customer and was photographed with one of the company’s meal coolers. The visibility helped take the business into a new phase. Other high profile customers such as Miranda Kerr and Cate Blanchett added to its profile while a nod from Gwyneth Paltrow gave the brand an international lift.Keep coming up with the next ideaGrowth wasn’t about settling into a nice routine. As the business grew to around 10,000 meals a week Monley searched for another way to improve the customer experience. The answer was a 100-acre farm that brought more transparency to how produce gets from field to table. Innovation, for Monley, doesn’t need to mean reinventing the wheel. It could be an improvement to an existing product, a response to customers or a smarter way to operate.Her journey from a Bondi kitchen to a multi-million dollar business has been a game of persistence. The numbers might be the milestones, but the real growth came from being clear on the purpose, learning when to ask for help, having setbacks and moving on.Images Courtesy: Bianca Monley WebsiteYou use AI every day. articles.body: This week’s OTT lineup features a mix of crime dramas, psychological thrillers, romance, and action. Viewers can explore police investigations in 'Eyes' and 'Pradhama Drishtiya Kuttakkar,' while 'Epic – First Semester' follows a young couple navigating love and future ambitions. Meanwhile, Vysakh's 'Khalifa: The Ruler' takes a textile shop owner into a dangerous world shaped by family history, gold trading, and power struggles. Here is what viewers can expect from each release and where to watch them.'Eyes'Stalking incidents involving women form the center of 'Eyes,' a thriller featuring Kani Kusruti as police officer Tina Sebastian. Her investigation takes her beyond the immediate details of the cases. She also examines the behavior and motivations that can turn obsession into a threat. The series explores questions of control, fixation, and the boundaries people cross in their relationships with others.Directed by Manu Ashokan, the thriller focuses on the psychological aspects of stalking alongside the police investigation. Tina must examine the circumstances surrounding the incidents to understand the people involved. Rather than focusing solely on the evidence, the narrative also considers the mindset behind such behavior. 'Eyes' premiered on SonyLIV on October 9.'Pradhama Drishtiya Kuttakkar'Parvathy Thiruvothu plays Aleena Abraham, a newly recruited police officer and mother whose life takes an unexpected turn after a fatal incident at her station. The incident raises questions that investigator Harris Meeran attempts to answer. As he examines the available clues, the possibility of a cover-up begins to emerge.The investigation develops into a psychological contest between Aleena and Harris. Each new detail could change how the case is understood, adding tension to their encounters. The story brings together a police investigation, personal complications, and questions surrounding the truth. 'Pradhama Drishtiya Kuttakkar' is a crime thriller that centers on the struggle to uncover what happened. The film, which has a 'Drishyam' vibe, began streaming on Netflix on October 9.'Epic – First Semester''Epic – First Semester' turns to romance and student life, following an aspiring filmmaker who moves abroad to pursue higher education. Anand Deverakonda plays Aditya, who travels to London for his master's degree. There, he meets Kadali, played by Vaishnavi Chaitanya, and the two enter a nine-month arrangement.Their relationship gradually becomes more complicated as their feelings develop. However, romance does not resolve the differences in their expectations or ambitions. Aditya and Kadali must consider how their individual plans could affect their future together. The Telugu romantic comedy explores the uncertainty that comes with relationships during a period of personal change. 'Epic – First Semester' arrived on Netflix on October 9.'Khalifa: The Ruler'Prithviraj Sukumaran stars as Aamir Ali, a textile shop owner whose routine life is disrupted by a gold-trading case involving his father. Looking for answers, Aamir begins investigating his family's past. His search leads him towards the legacy of his estranged grandfather and introduces him to a world of money, influence, and rivalries.'Khalifa: The Ruler' is scheduled to stream from October 9 on Prime Video and other platforms. articles.title: In 1929, Berlin’s planned birthday gift to Albert Einstein fell through; he built his own Caputh summer house, which became a meeting place for scientists, artists and thinkers
articles.summary: Albert Einstein turned 50 on 14 March 1929, and Berlin planned to mark the occasion by providing him with a country house.
articles.body: Albert Einstein turned 50 on 14 March 1929, and Berlin planned to mark the occasion by providing him with a country house. The proposed gift fell through after difficulties over the properties offered and became the subject of public controversy. Einstein subsequently secured a site in Caputh, near Potsdam, and financed the construction of a timber summer house designed by architect Konrad Wachsmann. The retreat became a place where he could read, think, sail and welcome friends away from the demands of public life. Einstein spent much of the year there between 1929 and 1932, and a guestbook associated with the house offers a glimpse of some of its visitors. Today, the property remains connected to his life and work, as well as to the political circumstances that forced him to leave Germany.Why Berlin’s birthday gift fell through, and how Einstein built his Caputh summer houseThe plan for a house originated with Berlin mayor Gustav Böss, who wanted to honour Einstein on his 50th birthday. However, the original property under consideration had tenants, whom Einstein did not want evicted. Other proposals followed, but the city did not provide him with a completed house. The dispute attracted press attention and became entangled in political arguments in Berlin, including antisemitic remarks. Elsa Einstein learned of a possible site in Caputh through their neighbours, Adolf and Elsbeth Stern. Adolf Stern had offered land from his property, and the proposed gift ultimately led Einstein to pursue a summer house there. Accounts of the property’s history indicate that the land-register arrangements involved Einstein’s stepdaughters, Ilse and Margot, so the transaction should not be described simply as Einstein personally registering the land in his own name.Elsa learned of a possible site in Caputh through friends who offered part of their property. Einstein chose the location and decided to proceed with the house, which was designed by the young architect Konrad Wachsmann. Einstein financed the construction himself. The building permit was applied for on 12 May 1929 and approved in June. The house was completed in time for the family to move in during September 1929.The house was built primarily of wood and designed as a relatively simple summer retreat rather than a grand residence. Konrad Wachsmann, a young architect at the time, was responsible for its design. The house provided Einstein with a quiet place away from public demands, with the surrounding landscape and nearby Havel lakes offering opportunities for walks and sailing. The house itself was not the birthday present Berlin had intended to provide. Einstein received a sailing boat named Tümmler for his 50th birthday, which he used on the nearby lakes.Einstein’s Caputh guestbook: Tagore, Max von Laue and other visitorsEinstein welcomed visitors from scientific, literary and cultural circles, and the family’s guestbook preserves a partial record of these encounters. The neighbouring Sterns gave the book to the family as a housewarming gift, and Einstein jokingly instructed guests to write in verse rather than ordinary prose.Among the figures associated with Einstein’s Caputh circle was the Indian poet and philosopher Rabindranath Tagore. The painter Hermann Struck illustrated a page of the guestbook in autumn 1931, and the page also bears the signature of Zionist leader Chaim Weizmann. Other visitors to Caputh included conductor Erich Kleiber and violinist Ruggiero Ricci, although their names should not be presented as guestbook entries unless independently verified. The original guestbook is held by the Leo Baeck Institute in New York.What happened to Einstein’s house after he left Germany?Einstein and Elsa left Caputh for the United States in December 1932. As the Nazi regime consolidated power, Einstein did not return to Germany. The house was searched on 20 March 1933. Accounts of its confiscation give different dates in 1935. Its subsequent history reflected the political upheavals of the period and changing decisions about how the property should be used and maintained. The East German Academy of Sciences restored the house in 1978–79, around the centenary of Einstein’s birth, and used it as a guest house and memorial. After German reunification, the Einstein Forum assumed administrative responsibility for the property in 1993. A later renovation, supported by the German federal government and the Cornelsen Culture Foundation, prepared the house for the Einstein Year in 2005. The Hebrew University of Jerusalem is the property’s majority owner.Today, Einstein’s summer house remains a place for historical reflection and intellectual exchange. Public access and guided tours depend on current arrangements, so visitors should confirm details with the Einstein Forum or the property’s administrator before travelling to Caputh. The house offers a glimpse of Einstein’s life away from public duties, but its history also reflects the antisemitic persecution that forced him to leave Germany and the later efforts to preserve the property as part of his legacy.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Plane hit, pilot killed: Riyadh airport attacks by Houthi kill three, damages Saudia aircraft
articles.summary: Three Saudi nationals were killed and several others injured in two attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and a Saudia Airlines aircraft
articles.body: Three Saudi nationals were killed and several others injured in two attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and a Saudia Airlines aircraft on Thursday, Saudi Arabia’s general authority of civil aviation said on Friday.The first attack targeted airport facilities, while the second struck the aircraft, the authority said. It did not identify those responsible, although Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen claimed to have targeted the airport, as cited by AP.Saudia Airlines has confirmed that a pilot was killed and an aircraft was damaged in the attack.Operations at King Khalid International Airport have since resumed, with air traffic returning to normal, according to the civil aviation authority.The attacks come amid a heightened security situation in Saudi Arabia following separate strikes on Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport on October 6 and 7. Those attacks left three people dead and 36 injured, according to the authority. Two people were killed and 28 injured at Abha airport, while one person was killed and eight injured at King Khalid International Airport.Saudi Civil Defence personnel responded to Thursday’s incident after a missile was launched by the Houthi militia, the Saudi Civil Defence said. Following the attacks on civilian facilities, Saudi-led coalition forces said they had destroyed 82 military targets belonging to the Houthi militia in Yemen.Amid the security situation, the Indian Embassy in Riyadh on Thursday advised Indian nationals in Saudi Arabia to remain vigilant, stay indoors when necessary and follow instructions issued by local authorities through official channels.“In view of the current situation, all Indian nationals in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia are advised to remain alert and vigilant, stay indoors as necessary, and follow the instructions issued by local authorities through official channels. Indian nationals are strongly advised to refrain from circulating or reposting any videos or news related to the ongoing events," the embassy said in an advisory.The mission said the Embassy of India in Riyadh and the Consulate in Jeddah, including their outsourced services through VFS, continued to operate normally and would issue further updates as required."The Embassy of India, Riyadh and the Consulate in Jeddah and its outsourced services through VFS, are continuing to function normally and will issue updates and advisories as and when necessary. The 24x7 helpline of Pravasi Bharatiya Sahayata Kendra (PBSK) remains available on Toll free No: 8002471234,” it added.India on Thursday condemned the attacks on the two Saudi airports, calling the targeting of civilian infrastructure “completely unacceptable”.In a statement, the Ministry of External Affairs said, “India condemns the attacks over the past few days targeting Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which have resulted in civilian deaths and injuries.”“The targeting of civilian infrastructure is completely unacceptable,” the MEA said, expressing condolences to the families of those killed and wishing those injured a speedy recovery.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: "We expected chaos in India": Norwegian mayor and his travel companion who travelled 43,000 km in a tuk-tuk share an unseen face of India
articles.summary: What happens when you trade the comfort of conventional travel for a three-wheeled auto-rickshaw and set out to cross India?
articles.body: What happens when you trade the comfort of conventional travel for a three-wheeled auto-rickshaw and set out to cross India? For Norwegian mayor Jo Inge Hesjevik and his travel companion Øyvind Hesjevik, the answer lies somewhere between breathtaking landscapes, unexpected encounters and chaotic Indian traffic.The duo recently took on the Rickshaw Run India, an adventure that saw them travel from Jaisalmer in Rajasthan to Fort Kochi in Kerala. The journey began on September 26 and culminated on October 9, covering a reported distance of approximately 4,300 km. The adventure also caught public attention after the Norwegian mayor was spotted travelling in a colourful auto-rickshaw in Gujarat.Organised by The Adventurists, the Rickshaw Run is not a conventional road trip with a fixed itinerary. Participants navigate their own way across the country in small auto-rickshaws, with the freedom to choose their routes and the possibility of unexpected mechanical and road challenges.The September 2026 edition officially ran from Jaisalmer to Fort KochiFor Øyvind, however, the journey was about much more than reaching the destination. In an exclusive interview with Times of India (Travel), he reflects on the experience of crossing India's changing landscapes, the lessons its roads taught him and why the country's warmth deserves to be experienced firsthand.When asked about their experience in India, Øyvind said, “We landed in Kochi with a mixture of relief and a bit of melancholy.”The relief came because we completed the journey without the auto-rickshaw breaking down, getting into a roadside accident or either traveller suffering from stomach problems. But there was also a sense of sadness that the adventure had come to an end.“The melancholy is because it is the end of a journey of daily experiences, challenges and encounters,” he explains.Travelling from north to south also gave the duo an opportunity to witness India's geographical and cultural diversity at close quarters. Rather than experiencing the country through a series of disconnected tourist attractions, they watched its landscapes and local cultures change as they moved between regions.Misconceptions about IndiaBefore arriving in India, they had certain ideas about what the country would look like. According to Øyvind, the image commonly presented back home often revolves around crowds at the Taj Mahal, congested streets, slum conditions and seemingly endless traffic jams.Another misconception, he says, is the tendency to view India as a geographical, cultural and culinary monolith.Their journey challenged these assumptions“Our experience has been very much contrary,” he says, recalling the variety of places they encountered, from Rajasthan's historic Silk Route towns and Gujarat's fertile fields to the mountainous landscapes and backwaters of India's southwest coast.For travellers, this is one of the most compelling reasons to explore India by road. A journey across different states can reveal how dramatically the scenery, food, architecture, traditions and everyday life change from one region to another.Rather than reducing the country to a handful of familiar landmarks, the road trip offered the duo a more layered understanding of India.What India's roads taught him about trafficWe can’t deny that Indian traffic can be intimidating for first-time visitors.“Even if ‘Indian traffic’ looks from the outside like unorganised chaos, once you get into it, it feels more like an intricate choreography,” he says. He believes there is a discernible hierarchy to the movement of traffic, even when the road appears chaotic to an outsider.That does not mean the experience was without its frightening moments. Buses, in particular, left him concerned about road safety.“The sound of the musical horns still makes me sweat in panic,” he admits.His experience captures an important part of travelling by road in India: the journey can be as challenging as it is rewarding. For visitors attempting a similar adventure, understanding local driving conditions, planning sensible daily distances and avoiding fatigue are essential.Did safety concerns match their experience?Before travelling to India, the group had also heard warnings about the possibility of women travellers facing harassment in public spaces.Øyvind says their experience differed from some of the concerns they had been told about. He travelled with Western female companions who had been advised to exercise considerable caution, but he describes their experience of moving around the country as one in which they felt safe and secure.When asked about the one thing Norwegians should experience in India, Øyvind said,“I think what people need to experience in person here is how welcoming the locals are to foreigners.”He believes that people in Western countries have something to learn from the openness and interest many Indians show towards visitors from other places.That warmth, combined with the everyday encounters that happen along the road, became a defining part of the journey.As the Rickshaw Run came to an end in Kochi, the travellers were left with memories of changing landscapes, challenging roads and conversations that no conventional itinerary could have guaranteed. Their experience is a reminder that sometimes the most revealing way to discover a country is to travel slowly, remain open to the unexpected and let the road lead the wayYou use AI every day. articles.title: Outsourced staff to submit data on 35,000 workers, warn of fresh stir if govt fails to act
articles.summary: Uttarakhand outsourced staff to submit data on 35,000 workers; govt promises action in 7 days on equal pay, regularisation, job security or protest resumes.
articles.body: Dehradun: Outsourced and contractual employees protesting in Dehradun agreed to submit department-wise details of workers to Uttarakhand govt after officials assured them that action on their demands would follow within seven days of receiving the data. The employees, who have been demanding equal pay, regularisation and job security, warned that they would resume their sit-in on the eighth day if govt failed to act.The agreement followed a meeting with state health secretary Vinay Shankar Pandey late Wednesday, during which officials sought information on outsourced employees across departments, including their length of service. Sanyukt Morcha Outsource Karmachari Sangh president Manglesh Lakhera said the union, which estimated that around 35,000 outsourced employees worked in Uttarakhand, would compile the information category-wise.“Officials said collecting the data themselves could take three to four months. We sought 15 to 20 days and will try to submit it within 15 days,” Lakhera said.The employees have been seeking equal pay for equal work, regularisation, continuity of service and an end to the outsourcing system. Their demands also include protection against arbitrary termination, timely salaries, EPF and ESI benefits, and implementation of Supreme Court’s Oct 26, 2016, ruling on equal pay for equal work.Lakhera said the administration had given several assurances, including a proposed meeting with chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami. Officials also indicated that the outsourcing system could be revised to allow departments to engage workers directly instead of through intermediary contractors, while an order would be issued to prevent arbitrary termination.“The govt has assured us that action will follow within seven days. If that does not happen, we will resume our sit-in on the eighth day,” Lakhera said.The protest had earlier received support from Uttarakhand Kranti Dal, Swabhiman Morcha and Congress.Stay updated with the latest Dehradun news.
